findings.title: Findings converge on how D6 writes needs-restart onto the entry that set_status owns
findings.why_it_matters: D6 (fold the needs-restart flag into the FAILED instance entry, as HA does with `FAILED_UNLOAD`) moves the flag from a separate record onto the entry that `set_status` now rebuilds on every write. Three findings, from both critics, each add a clause to that one contract. Finding 2: nothing in `set_status` keeps the flag when the entry is rewritten. Finding 3: the flag is a second write after the FAILED write, outside `set_status`. Finding 4: the entry has nowhere to keep the class name the old record stored. Each proposes its own patch to D6. Together they suggest D6 settled *where* the flag lives but not *how it is written and kept* under a single writer. Should that write contract be worked out once, before the three are patched one at a time? The re-evaluation is open-ended. It can also conclude that the ratified D6 text plus a sentence or two is enough.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate how D6's flag is written under `set_status` before addressing Findings 2, 3 and 4 individually. Open questio
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate how D6's flag is written under `set_status` before addressing Findings 2, 3 and 4 individually.

findings.title: set_status doesn't enforce D6's rule that a flagged entry is never overwritten or removed
findings.why_it_matters: Today the flag survives `unregister_app` and `record_failure` because it lives in a separate dict (`flag_needs_restart` docstring). Under D6 it lives on the entry that `set_status(FAILED)` rebuilds and `set_status(STOPPED)` deletes. D6's ratified text makes the protection a per-caller promise ("stop, discard and prune never remove a flagged entry"), while the design's premise is a single writer. If a FAILED write builds a fresh entry without the flag, `flag_needs_restart`'s "first record stands" check reads the wiped entry and returns True. That replaces the original reason and time, and flips `record_flagged_outcome` from `refused` to `failed`. A STOPPED write on a flagged entry removes the guard against owner-id collisions (specs 138-140).
findings.recommended: A: State the invariant in D6 and the `set_status` contract: a FAILED write over a flagged entry keeps the original flag, an

findings.title: The flag is a second write after FAILED, so FAILED-without-flag is a state the design allows
findings.why_it_matters: Each settle site writes FAILED, then flags, then sends (`settle_raised_shutdown`, `settle_failed_init`, `settle_failed_stop`). D6 says flagging "isn't a transition", so no `StatusChange` exists for it, and the UI learns about the flag only because `on_app_state_changed` re-reads the registry when it handles the event. That holds only while every site flags before it emits. The design adds a second ordering rule: `set_status` must come before the flag, or the flag has no entry to sit on. The flag write must also get past D5's change detection, because it is a rewrite of a FAILED entry.
findings.recommended: A: Flagging becomes a parameter of the FAILED `set_status` write; the separate flag mutator goes away and its "first record

findings.title: A flagged entry has no class name once NeedsRestartRecord is deleted
findings.why_it_matters: `NeedsRestartRecord.class_name` exists "so the row still renders after its entry is unregistered or its app leaves config". `InstanceEntry` has no class name. `_info_from_entry` takes a FAILED entry's class name from the manifest, or `"Unknown"` when there is none. Under D6 the entry is never unregistered, so that half of the reason goes away. A flagged instance whose app is removed from the config would still render as `Unknown`. Related build item: `flagged_app_keys` (used by database retention to keep removed apps' rows) reads `_needs_restart` and has to be re-derived from entries. D6's diff list doesn't name it.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a flagged instance whose app leaves the config shows its class as "Unknown" until restart.

findings.title: Deleting the re-send loop leaves no repair for a FAILED event that fails to send
findings.why_it_matters: The frontend's `appStatus` cache takes priority over refetched manifests (`instanceLiveStatus`), and only a WS reconnect clears it. `transition()` logs and swallows a send failure. If a FAILED event is lost, the UI keeps the old status until the next start of that app or a reconnect. The old loop re-sent every current failure on each start. Both critics also argue that bus delivery can reorder events. Synthesis checked that claim and found it doesn't hold against D2. The deleted loop re-sent only FAILED snapshots (`app_lifecycle_start_stop.py:197-198`), so it never repaired a reordered STARTING/RUNNING pair. D4 also doesn't add events: it swaps today's NOT_STARTED event (`:208`) for STARTING, so a start still sends two. In addition, the dispatch loop spawns handler tasks in event order (`bus_service.py:490`), and the handler's only await path ends in an `asyncio.Lock` (FIFO) and `put_nowait` (`runtime_query_service.py:494-505`). Reordering was not shown to happen.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: a FAILED event whose send fails (logged at ERROR) leaves that row stale until the app's ne
findings.chosen: C: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: Reading a missing entry as NOT_STARTED turns racing writes at exit into apparent changes
findings.why_it_matters: `set_status` infers the from-state of an absent entry (D3), and its only dedupe is "nothing changed". Any write onto an absent entry therefore looks like a change from NOT_STARTED. When a runtime stop and `shutdown_all` both settle one instance, the second STOPPED reports NOT_STARTED → STOPPED. The second FAILED compares a freshly built `TimeoutError`/`RuntimeError` (`settle_failed_stop`) and emits again. A STOPPING write from `stop_one` onto an instance a runtime stop already removed creates a short-lived entry. An `initialize_instance` that finishes after `clear_all()` writes RUNNING into an empty registry. The design doesn't say what `set_status` does on an absent entry for any `to` other than NOT_STARTED.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: when process exit overlaps a runtime stop or start, a racing write can emit a duplicate ev

findings.title: D4's claim that snapshot counts stop counting initializing instances as running is false
findings.why_it_matters: `tally_app_statuses` counts `AppManifestInfo.status`. `build_manifest_info` derives that status as `has_running = any(not is_failed_info(info))`, and `is_failed_info` checks only `error` and `needs_restart`. So a NOT_STARTED, STARTING or STOPPING instance counts as running exactly as before, and the app row says RUNNING while its instance rows say STARTING. `AppStatus` has no STARTING member (`wire/src/hassette_wire/enums.py:87-106`), so changing that is a wire-enum change. Synthesis also found two more snapshot-side points D4 and D3 don't mention. First, `_info_from_entry` reports a live entry's status from `app.status` (the App resource's own status, the second holder in D8), not from the entry (`app_registry.py:411`). Second, a configured name with no entry gets a synthetic STOPPED row (`:498-504`), while the next event's `previous_status` is NOT_STARTED (D3).

findings.title: set_status and transition() are two separate calls at every write site
findings.why_it_matters: D1's deciding factor is "no write can skip its event", but D1 closes that only for the factory. Everywhere else the pattern is `change = registry.set_status(...)` followed by `await self.transition(change)`, at about a dozen sites (the Summary's list). Dropping the returned change, or writing from a sync helper that can't await, is the silent write D1 rejected option B for. `prune_stale_failed` returning changes for the caller to emit is the same shape. Two of the sites are sync today (`settle_failed_init`, `settle_failed_stop`), which write and leave the send to the caller.
findings.recommended: A: Give `AppInstanceLifecycleMixin` one async method that calls `registry.set_status` and emits the result. Lifecycle code
findings.chosen: A: Give AppInstanceLifecycleMixin one async method that calls registry.set_status and emits the result

findings.title: Registration is silent, so queued siblings keep showing STOPPED after a stop or reload
findings.why_it_matters: Today a NOT_STARTED event goes out for each newly created instance before the instances initialize one by one (`app_lifecycle_start_stop.py:204-208`, `:466`). Under D4 and D3, registering onto a missing entry is NOT_STARTED → NOT_STARTED, which is no change, so no event goes out. The critic's main example doesn't hold: synthesis checked that a configured failed name keeps its FAILED entry until it is overwritten (start prunes only names outside the config, `:150-162`), so retrying a failed app writes FAILED → NOT_STARTED. That is a change, and it emits. What remains: after a clean stop or the stop half of a reload, the entry is gone, so each queued sibling keeps showing STOPPED until its own STARTING.
findings.recommended: A: Add to D4's accepting clause that, after a stop or reload, queued siblings show STOPPED until their own STARTING event.
findings.chosen: A: Add to D4's accepting clause

findings.title: The design doesn't say whether the STARTING send counts against the startup timeout
findings.why_it_matters: D4 puts the STARTING write and its awaited event just before `inst.initialize()`, which runs inside `anyio.fail_after(self.startup_timeout)`. If the send is inside that block, a slow bus eats the app's startup budget, and a timeout there is reported as an app init failure.
findings.chosen: Add one sentence to D4: the STARTING transition is written and sent before `initialize_instance` opens `anyio.fail_after(self.startup_timeout)`, so the event send never counts against the app's startup timeout.

findings.title: Cancellation between a status write and its event or init's end leaves the entry at the last written status
findings.why_it_matters: `initialize_instance` catches only `Exception`. A `CancelledError` during the STARTING send or during init leaves the entry at STARTING with a live App and no error, and siblings not yet reached stay NOT_STARTED. Likewise, a `CancelledError` inside `transition()` is a `BaseException`, so it escapes "logged, never raised" after the registry has already changed, and the UI and registry disagree. In the current code, a cancelled init leaves the registry saying RUNNING (registration writes RUNNING), which is just as wrong, so this isn't a regression.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: cancellation between a status write and its event or init's end (in practice, process exit
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: cancellation between a status write and its event or init's end (in practice, process exit

findings.title: D7's "after every running instance has already sent" isn't true for one registered after shutdown_all begins
findings.why_it_matters: D7's justification says `clear_all()` runs after every running instance has emitted its own STOPPED or FAILED. `shutdown_all` collects instances once, at its start (`app_lifecycle_instances.py:478-480`), and takes no app-key lock. An instance a runtime start registers after that point is cleared without any event. The stance (send nothing at exit) holds either way. Only the sentence that will go into the docstring and the PR overstates it.
findings.recommended: A: Reword D7 (and the planned docstring and PR text) to "after every instance registered when `shutdown_all` began has sent

findings.title: D5's identity comparison dedupes nothing, because no site passes the same exception twice
Findings converge on process exit's lock-free teardown racing in-flight lifecycle writes
findings.why_it_matters: `shutdown_all` takes its list of live instances once and stops them without taking any app-key lock (app_lifecycle_instances.py:501-503; D7). Meanwhile a start, reload or stop can still be running under its lock. `set_status` is left as the only thing that settles the interleaved writes. Findings 2-5 are four symptoms of that one arrangement. A sibling torn down mid-start still gets initialized (2). A late RUNNING overwrites STOPPING (3). A stale writer's STOPPED can delete a replacement's entry (4). A teardown that settles after `clear_all` leaves a ghost FAILED entry (5). Each proposes its own guard in `set_status` or the lifecycle. The branch already added one such guard: the `_record_created` flag re-check (Build call, app_lifecycle_start_stop.py:188-210). `fail_needs_restart`'s "already flagged, report as refusal" path exists for the same reason. Does this point to a problem with how exit interleaves with in-flight lifecycle work, one that should be decided once instead of guarded write by write? Re-evaluation is open-ended. It can also conclude that every exit-time race is an accepted limitation, since `clear_all` discards the registry straight afterwards, and document that in one place.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the exit interleaving
findings.chosen: 3: Lock-free, accept + fix F2 (after a prior-art check: design/research/2026-11-14-exit-vs-inflight-lifecycle/prior-art.md)

findings.title: A refused status write is invisible to its caller, so `initialize_instance` initializes an App whose entry is gone or flagged
findings.why_it_matters: `set_app_status` returns `None` for every case `set_status` returns `None` for: nothing changed, a write dropped onto a missing entry, and a write refused onto a flagged entry (app_lifecycle_instances.py:136-166; app_registry.py:129-142). Its docstring says "a caller that needs to know whether a write landed checks the registry". Only `_record_created` does. `initialize_instance` writes STARTING, then runs `inst.initialize()` and records `succeeded` whatever happened (:106-134). At process exit, `shutdown_all` lists NOT_STARTED siblings too (they hold their App). It writes STOPPING and tears sibling B down, which removes B's entry or flags it. When the `initialize_instances` loop reaches B, STARTING is dropped, `initialize()` runs on a torn-down App, RUNNING is dropped, and the outcome says succeeded. In the flagged case `set_status` logs the WARNING that, by D6's write contract, "marks a real bug, not routine traffic". Synthesis checked: the old code also initialized a sibling `shutdown_all` had already stopped, since it registered RUNNING eagerly and the loop didn't re-check. The torn-down init is therefore not new. The misleading WARNING and the "check the registry" contract that no caller follows are new. The data-integrity sub-claim about `_discard_failed_instances` does not hold: it touches only unflagged FAILED entries, which `shutdown_all` never lists, so nothing can flag them mid-loop.
findings.recommended: A

findings.title: A late RUNNING write can overwrite STOPPING, so the stored status goes backwards at exit
findings.why_it_matters: `set_status` accepts RUNNING onto a STOPPING entry that still holds its App. That write is in `LIVE_STATUSES`, the App is present, and the status differs, so it is a change (app_registry.py:129-176). During `shutdown_all`, a STARTING instance gets STOPPING (:483). When its in-flight `initialize()` finishes, `initialize_instance` writes RUNNING (:134) and emits STOPPING → RUNNING. The UI row reads RUNNING during teardown until STOPPED arrives. If the stop is cancelled, RUNNING is the last status stored and sent until `clear_all`.
findings.recommended: B

findings.title: `set_status` has no writer identity, so a stale writer's STOPPED can remove a replacement instance's entry
findings.why_it_matters: Entries are keyed by `(app_key, name)` only. A STOPPED from instance A's teardown removes whatever entry holds the name, including a replacement B registered after A's stop began. RUNNING, STOPPING and FAILED overwrite the same way (app_registry.py:141-174). B then runs untracked: `holds_app` is false and it is out of `get_live_apps`. `shutdown_instance`'s `finally` already compares identity (`registry.get(...) is not inst`), which shows the question exists. The old unregister path was equally name-keyed. The senior-engineer critic disputes the fix as over-engineered, since the app-key lock covers every runtime path. Synthesis notes that in the one concrete trigger (a reload's restart racing `shutdown_all`'s join of the old teardown), B is outside `shutdown_all`'s list anyway, so D7 already accepts that it gets cleared without a stop, and an identity guard wouldn't stop B either.
findings.recommended: B

findings.title: A teardown that settles after `clear_all` re-creates a FAILED entry
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a long-lived process where `clear_all` is not the last registry operation. FAILED is in `MISSING_ENTRY_STATUSES` (app_registry.py:37-40) for create-time failures (D1, D3). A `settle_*` FAILED or the phantom handler running after `clear_all` therefore creates a new FAILED entry in a registry that was just cleared. The `clear_all` docstring implies nothing is left. At exit this is invisible. In the harness, `reset_app_handler` awaits `stop_app` for every app before `clear_all` (testing/_reset.py:106-113), so a leak needs a stop started outside that loop, for example a test-spawned background task.
findings.recommended: B

findings.title: The frontend's "degraded" rollup counts only `running` as healthy, and its comment still describes a binary registry
findings.why_it_matters: `appLiveStatus` returns "degraded" only when a `"running"` and a `"failed"` instance coexist (frontend/src/utils/app-data.ts:141). Otherwise it takes the worst status by priority, and `failed` (0) beats `starting` (4), `stopping` (6) and `not_started` (9) (status-priority.ts:14-25). The server counts any non-failed instance as running (`build_manifest_info`, app_registry.py:483-484), so it says DEGRADED where the UI row says "failed". The comment at app-data.ts:110-115 says this mirrors "`AppRegistry`'s own binary model ... an instance entry is either running or failed". This branch makes that comment false: entries now store NOT_STARTED, STARTING and STOPPING. Synthesis checked the critic's regression claim against origin/main and it does not hold. The old code also sent a NOT_STARTED event for every new instance (origin/main app_lifecycle_start_stop.py:208, :466), and old snapshots reported `app.status` (origin/main app_registry.py:411). So "failed" showing for failed + not-started predates the branch. What the branch adds is the false comment, and more intermediate statuses on the wire.
findings.recommended: A
findings.choice_reason: option A and then file an issue for option B?

findings.title: `needs_restart` on the WS message is read from the registry when the event is handled, and the docstring's reason for that no longer holds
findings.why_it_matters: `RuntimeQueryService.on_app_state_changed` calls `registry.resolve_instance_info` at handling time and stamps the flag it finds onto the payload (runtime_query_service.py:212-231). Its docstring justifies that "so no emit site can drop it". This branch reduces the emit sites to one, `set_app_status`, so the stated reason is gone. The behavior: an earlier event (STARTING, say) handled after a flagged FAILED write lands carries the flag, so the UI briefly shows a starting row with a needs-restart badge until the FAILED message arrives. The frontend only ever adds a flag (`entry?.needs_restart ?? inst.needs_restart`, app-data.ts:180; use-websocket.ts:145), so this errs toward showing the flag and self-corrects. The read predates the branch (runtime_query_service.py is not in the diff). The branch adds STARTING events, so there are more earlier events in flight.
findings.recommended: B
findings.choice_reason: fix it small now, file an issue? it does sound like adding it to the event is the right call, yeah?

findings.title: The squash title and footer carry no breaking-change marker for user-visible event and API changes
findings.why_it_matters: Users can observe these changes. `HassetteAppStateEvent` is exported (events/__init__.py:23, 49), and its `from_app`/`from_instance_info` classmethods are gone. Their replacement `from_change` takes the core-internal `StatusChange`, so `hassette.testing` is the only supported path. A first start no longer emits NOT_STARTED (the old code sent one per new instance, origin/main app_lifecycle_start_stop.py:208, 466). Instances now emit STARTING, and NOT_STARTED appears only on a retry after a failure. docs/pages/core-concepts/bus/methods.md:289 now documents the new sequence. The commits are plain `feat:`/`fix:` with no `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. CLAUDE.md requires `feat!:` plus one footer, and migration guidance for API changes even with zero in-repo callers.
findings.chosen: When the PR is created, title it `feat!: ...` and end the body with exactly one `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer naming: the removal of `HassetteAppStateEvent.from_app` and `from_instance_info` (build events through the `hassette.testing` simulate helpers instead); the new STARTING event; and that NOT_STARTED is no longer sent on a first start, only on a retry over a failed instance.

findings.title: Only a lost FAILED event is an accepted limitation, but lost RUNNING, STOPPING and STOPPED events strand the UI the same way
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a deployment where in-process event sends can fail. D2 accepts that a FAILED event whose send raises leaves the row stale until the next start or a WS reconnect. `set_app_status` treats every status the same way, logging the failure and moving on (app_lifecycle_instances.py:158-166). So a lost RUNNING leaves the UI at STARTING while the registry says RUNNING, and the frontend cache outranks refetched manifests (app-data.ts:154). The critic's out-of-order concern was checked in the sketch challenge (review-log finding 5) and not shown to happen.
findings.recommended: B
findings.choice_reason: what are your thoughts? whats the proper fix for this?

findings.title: Snapshots still derive "failed" from `error`/`needs_restart`, not from the stored status
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger's goal is one stored truth per instance. `is_failed_info` (schemas/app_snapshots.py:157-159) decides failure from `info.error is not None or info.needs_restart is not None`, and `build_manifest_info` and the manifest counts use it (app_registry.py:483-484, 506, 550; app_snapshots.py:93, 98), not `info.status`. Today the two agree. `_info_from_entry` sets `status=FAILED` exactly when it sets `error` (app_registry.py:419-443), and `set_status` requires an error for FAILED. Two rules decide the same fact, and the agreement rests on an invariant stated elsewhere. The function predates the branch, but this branch makes `status` the stored truth.
findings.recommended: A
